newsitem.title: GERMANY: Italy's Ciampi sees Italy joining EMU on time.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Ciampi sees Italy joining EMU on time.

text.p: Italy will be among the nations which qualify for European Monetary Union in 1999, Italy's Treasury and Budget Minister Carlo Azeglio Ciampi said on Sunday in an interview with German newspaper Welt am Sonntag.

Ciampi, known as "Superminister" because of his combined ministry, said: "We will present ourselves in the kind of condition which will ensure a positive decision," when the decision is made in 1998 about who qualifies for EMU.

Ciampi served as prime minister for 11 months in 1993/94 and was also governor of Italy's Central Bank for 14 years. In May of this year he was given the combined treasury and budget ministry by Italy's Prime Minister Romano Prodi.

Italy would not use a possible loosening of fiscal requirements to meet the tough financial criteria established in the Maastricht Treaty for countries wishing to participate in currency union in 1999, Ciampi said.
To join EMU, countries must show their inflation rates are low, currencies are stable and deficits are at low levels.
Ciampi said that the parameters set out in the Maastricht Treaty should be strictly followed to avoid possibly weakening the single currency.
"It is in Europe's best interests to have a strong Euro. We couldn't allow the strong deutschemark to be replaced by a weak Euro," said Ciampi.

When it comes to Italy's massive government debt ratio, however, Ciampi said it was a question of establishing a trend of debt reduction, rather than exactly fulfilling government debt criteria as laid out in the Maastricht Treaty.
"There is different emphasis on government debt ratios than on the other three convergence criteria. It is a question of the country showing a trend towards reducing the debt," said Ciampi.
"Our country owes more than two trillion marks. Getting this level of debt down from 120 percent of GDP to 60 percent of GDP in the near future is out of the question.

"But other countries are showing signs of not achieving the 60 percent ratio either. The outcome of this seems to be that the 60 percent ratio will not be mechanically enforced, but it is the the trend towards getting government debt ratios will count," said Ciampi.
Italy would meet the inflation criteria set out in the Maastricht Treaty, Ciampi said, and he expected Italy's average inflation rate by the end of the year to be under three percent.
"This means it is enough next year to take inflation down another half a percent. This is the fruit of what I call the culture of stability," said Ciampi.
The most important measure towards getting Italy on the road to EMU was the reform of the pension system, which the country began a year and a half ago.
"Some people say this does not go far enough. We have decided, however, to have a check-up three years after its introduction.
"If the step-by-step increase in the minimum pensionable age is not enough, then after the check-up we can introduce further measures," said Ciampi.
